Italy’s future is debated in schools, barracks and state governments. Support for unification need not entail hostility to France; protection cannot answer local questions of revenue and political standing.

Italian political mobilisation has changed local government. Established republics and newly organised republican forces seek cooperation, while military costs, revenue and representation remain matters for concrete negotiation.

The Italian states have different governments, armies and foreign ties. The Lombard Republic endures with French support, while republican conviction, dynastic interests and local finances shape the road ahead. The states may pursue unification or lasting cooperation through public obligations.

Manchu and Mongol communities have left for [SCOPE.sCountry('nesnd_a2_cne_country').GetName] or the west of [SCOPE.sCountry('nesnd_a2_usa_country').GetName]. Each community has a seventy percent chance of choosing the former and thirty percent the latter. Community sizes differ, so the actual population is not divided in an exact seventy-to-thirty ratio.

No receiving destination remains in the American west. The Manchu and Mongol communities have all moved to [SCOPE.sCountry('nesnd_a2_cne_country').GetName], and the planned division between two destinations has not taken place.
Neither destination can receive the Manchu and Mongol communities. They remain where they live, and this migration has ended. The registration choice already enacted remains in force.

No receiving destination remains in the east. The Manchu and Mongol communities have all moved to western [SCOPE.sCountry('nesnd_a2_usa_country').GetName], and the planned division between two destinations has not taken place.
Community militias and dynastic supporters have broken with our government and established their own. Their claims to land and old compacts now confront the armies of both states.

[SCOPE.sCountry('nesnd_restoration_applicant').GetName] proposes recognizing the existing Inca court and joining our state. Union would end the partition and bring its local communities into the political settlement we must uphold.
The Inca court did not consent to union within the allotted time. Both states retain their governments and territory. Negotiations may be renewed after the waiting period.
The Inca court has declined the union offer. A shared dynastic tradition has not proved sufficient to end the partition. Talks may resume after the waiting period.
Preserve the state and renew its compact.

Dynastic supporters have reconvened the local communities to settle relations among court, local representatives, and countryside. The existing state will continue under a renewed political compact, bearing the divisions left by the earlier war.

Indigenous communities displaced by repression have crossed the border, bringing family ties, local organizations, and memories of lost homes. Their destinations will anchor new refuge networks, though arrival does not immediately restore their livelihoods.

The army has dispersed the restoration movement, but the rural conflict persists. Families with a receiving destination begin to leave; those without one remain. Political representatives enter exile, while disputes over land and local authority endure.

The old dynasty has returned to the center of political life. Local communities have offered their support in pursuit of recognition for their land and representatives. Relations among court, assembly, and countryside will now develop under the new settlement.
Take responsibility for the country left by war.
The opposing government has lost its final territories and the war demand has been enforced. The united state inherits these lands together with the local conflicts and exile left by the war.

The struggle has ended without reunification under our government. Surviving governments retain their actual territories, and dynastic claims have not become accomplished facts merely because fighting has stopped.

The heirs of Moctezuma and the Andean court claim different inheritances. Both confront a question the republics have left unresolved: can Indigenous communities control their land and local government? Dynastic supporters appeal to old compacts, while rural communities resist dispossession. Recognition, negotiation, and repression offer sharply different futures.

French-backed republican projects, the Italian dynasties and papal power make unification a question for the European order. Austria can protect independent states through defensive agreements or bear the cost of intervention in a territorial dispute.\n\nA divided Italy is not the only possible outcome. Recognizing a new unifying power also means accepting limits to Vienna’s influence. Every decision must reckon with existing treaties, armies and interests.
No Italian territorial dispute is currently available for Austrian intervention.

Three months of mutual fulfilment establish an accord. An unanswered proposal lapses after ninety days; talks may resume after twelve months.

The Lombard Republic has French support, but the Italian states retain their own revenues, armies and schools. Development can proceed under protection; both unification and lasting cooperation require concrete local commitments. French political credit cannot decide on another state’s behalf.

Building a common Italy means reckoning with the states’ existing military obligations and taxes. Industrial interests favour pooled resources; local traders want revenue kept for schools, and the army puts military accounts and veterans first. A common budget must reconcile these burdens, whether the states pursue unification or negotiate a lasting relationship among themselves.

Faced with concrete diplomatic obstacles, the government proposes cooperation through the states’ own budgets and commitments. Existing workshops and schools remain; relations with France will determine future policy.

The Lombard Republic allows French support and Italian integration to proceed together. Republican institutions, public works and talks with each state will underpin this course. French credit does not replace their consent.

Support lasting cooperation through local schools, religious responsibilities and the states’ own revenues. The government favours shared public obligations; future unification remains for the states to pursue through politics and diplomacy.
The southern approach connects dynastic continuity with local revenue and military arrangements. Supporting it changes no existing government and grants no licence to annex neighbours.

French support for the Lombard Republic gave the republican cause a foothold in Italy. Orders for workshops, credit for merchants and funds for schools must still be found within Italy. The army presses for military works, merchants seek dependable repayment, and local contributors want places for their children. The government’s spending will help determine whose needs take priority.

[SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] asks France to lend political credit to its Italian programme for six years. Its supporters hope French prestige will persuade domestic and foreign interests to accept the undertaking. The commitment itself does not alter the sovereignty of the Italian states.
A diplomatic proposal has reached the government. The envoy awaits an answer.

A neighbouring state proposes a shared public undertaking. Schools, local revenues and military expenses would become budgetary obligations for both governments. Each must fund services on its own territory. The proposal preserves both states and their borders; the decision is ours.

The other government is willing to negotiate, but asks that schools and local services take precedence over military commitments. Both states would still fund and operate their own establishments. A letter of assent cannot replace those obligations.
The states have failed to settle the obligations of this undertaking. Each remains responsible for its schools, revenue and military expenditure; further talks must await another occasion.

Both governments have maintained the promised services and borne the expenditure. Their cooperation now rests on something tangible in local life. Unification and lasting cooperation between states remain political choices.

Let the next generation inherit it.

A generation of Egyptians has lived through thirty years of independent government. Foreign merchants retain their property and the powers retain their ambitions, but the government has preserved the right to choose the country’s course. Its future factories and schools can give that right firmer foundations.

The dynasty has accepted its investment partner’s protection. The support brought in for factories, armaments and schools has become a relationship that constrains national sovereignty. The government still rules Egypt, but must now find its place within a different order.
The government must answer for this.

Egypt’s room for independent action has been exhausted, with no current investment partner to assume its protection. Earlier development and transactions remain, but the dynasty can no longer appeal to outside support as evidence that it can preserve independence.

An eligible investment partner remains, but the protection relationship could not be established. The government must acknowledge the failure of the settlement. The dynasty must continue to govern Egypt without using that unfulfilled guarantee to justify its independence policy.
Let learning and production grow together.

Universities are training specialists, while tooling workshops and a major industry have filled their workplaces. Ambitions once written in agreements are gaining substance through Egyptian teaching and labour. Capital may move; the capabilities established here deserve continued cultivation.

Egypt has become subject to another overlord. The former investment arrangement has lost its basis, bringing this test of independence to an end. The government’s future position must now be determined by its actual subject relationship.
A valid investment commitment costs 1 Independence each month. Changing partners does not reset Independence or the thirty-year term.

When Independence is exhausted, Egypt accepts a qualified investment partner’s protection. If no partner can undertake it, or the relationship cannot be established, the dynasty bears the political cost of the failed guarantee.
The independence settlement has endured for thirty years

The settlement of 1825 recognized Egypt’s release from Ottoman rule. Six powers guaranteed its independence in return for investment rights along the Nile. The dynasty gained breathing room, while its factories, schools and army acquired new creditors.\n\nForeign machinery and teachers can strengthen Egypt; foreign control of its economy can also erode its freedom of action. The government may choose a partner or withdraw its political commitment. Whether Egypt can still determine its own future after thirty years will depend on those choices and the economic order they leave behind.
Schools and Workshops of the Nile

Machinery can be purchased more quickly than a country can train the people who build, repair and operate it. Universities must educate local specialists, tooling workshops must supply equipment, and new industries must attract workers.\n\nThe government seeks an enduring foundation for Egyptian power. Whatever the source of its capital, an institution must teach and a factory must employ people before a promise becomes a national capability.

Choose a principal investment partner from the surviving, independent signatories able to undertake Egypt’s protection, seeking lasting support through construction, education and industry. Three German states now cooperate with us through real agreements. The army and armaments industry give common defence a material foundation. The states retain their own governments, and the value of their cooperation depends on continued observance.

Our government must decide its response through the diplomatic play now before it.

The order that constrained the German states has changed. Unification or the retreat of outside domination has established a new standing for our country. Earlier cooperation has left political and military experience, while the future order remains to be shaped.
Austria has joined the defending side in the Italian dispute. Diplomatic assurances now carry military and financial commitments, and Vienna’s prestige will share in the outcome.

The opposing power has accepted demands in this dispute, and the protected state has preserved its position. Austria’s voice in Italian affairs has gained renewed support.

Austria’s intervention has failed to preserve the position it sought to defend. Territorial demands, subordination or the disappearance of the protected state have undone the original commitment. Vienna must face the consequences in Italy.

Half of the Indigenous populations remaining in the two source countries have joined it after cession. The new khan inherits the memory of an earlier uprising and faces intervention against the new order.

Schools have opened their doors, but inherited status still determines how far their pupils may rise. Appointing officers and officials by ability requires both new laws and education for families once excluded from it.
Support local opponents of colonial rule as they prepare to rise.

Pay £5,000 and increase government wage costs by 2%. Organisation grows where turmoil is high or living standards are below 10. Transport, the extent of unrest and French officers affect its pace. Pausing ends maintenance and loses 2 preparation each month.

An envoy from [SCOPE.sCountry('india_sender').GetName] has brought a formal proposal. Our existing relations do not commit us to unconditional support. We must decide what responsibility we are prepared to accept.

The dynasty’s old prestige still carries weight, but its subjects also judge their sovereign by the conduct of government. Respect for the provinces’ faiths and the court’s ability to make its own decisions will shape their loyalty.
Support for the Dynasty has reached 60.

France has not come to secure India’s independence. Yet borrowed knowledge can become a strength of our own. Teachers, engineers and officers may be invited; whether they come depends on what Paris is prepared to invest in the relationship.
Foreign assistance calls for a policy of our own.

Bengali cloth reaches distant markets, yet the imperial army still relies on ageing equipment. Mines, toolworks and railways can bring these scattered resources together. The arsenals need not supply every purchase, but they must produce more than figures in a ledger.

Pay £20,000 to support the rising. A local state is formed. Its former ruler demands the return of this state; the insurgents demand humiliation. An independent sponsor joins the insurgents. Sponsorship does not grant ownership of their land.

Delhi, Nanjing and Paris each have terms to offer the Indian princes. Their rulers seek to preserve more than ancestral palaces: land, revenue and the right to decide their own future are at stake. Cooperation may bring assistance without securing independence.
Our sovereignty and local interests must be defended.

Concentrate the court’s staff and funding on this undertaking.
Make this our reform priority. The other programme pauses without losing its gains.

The old Mughal empire relied on the prestige of its sovereigns to bind the provinces together. Its rulers now face different demands. French merchants and officers have brought wealth and new weapons, along with new creditors. The state needs schools and workshops of its own to turn provincial revenues into the means to defend it.
The court is establishing schools and workshops.
Provide a grant and four years of specialist assistance. The recipient pays the advisers’ expenses. The mission withdraws if the countries go to war or the recipient changes its overlord.
Increase the recipient’s autonomy by one level.
Conclude a defensive pact with a three-year binding period.
Recognise independence and establish a five-year truce.
Our state will join the other country, bringing its lands and people into the union.

The dispute has ended, and we retain the territory of the rising as an independent state.
Our former ruler demands this land back. Negotiation and war will decide its independence. Foreign assistance must not become another country’s excuse to annex us.

The empire needs officials who can read its accounts and teachers who can educate the next generation. One college in Delhi cannot serve every province. Paper, teachers and regular funding must reach the districts together.
Give the provinces’ shared political demands a place in the constitution.

Living under one government does not make its subjects a nation. The provinces have their own languages, faiths and princes. As schools and cities grow, their inhabitants are asking who can speak for India. Dynasties, local leaders and the emerging national movement must each offer an answer.
The provinces are seeking a common political home.
Devote additional policing resources to disrupting local organisations.

Unification has erased borders without erasing differences between the provinces. The new state must sustain taxation, education and public services if its common laws are to mean anything beyond the court.
Offer one state terms for joining India. It may refuse. Acceptance requires a settlement payment and ten years of princely pensions.

The Southern Court relies on ports, garrisons and local allies to sustain its rule. Its opponents also need organisation, money and friends. Delhi can assist them without treating their lands as its reward.

The Southern Court’s Indian possessions lie across the ocean, where merchants, garrisons and local princes pursue different interests. Nanjing may govern them directly or place them under a separate commission. Neither arrangement can improve local livelihoods by decree alone.
Sea routes connect Tianzhu to the Southern Court’s market.

Japan shall decide its own affairs.

Envoys from Nanjing have brought new terms. Kyoto and Osaka would recognize the Emperor, with a regent conducting the government; the Tokugawa would rule from Edo, the Toyotomi would retain a reduced western domain, and Wu would administer Kyushu and Shikoku directly. The mainland court whose armies helped establish Toyotomi power now proposes to divide it. Retainers have reported the strength and supplies of the garrisons to [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetFullName], who must decide how to answer.

Japan asks the court to withdraw the partition proposal and retain a unified Toyotomi government. The proposed expedition would establish new Japanese governments and divide the forces and revenues now commanded by the Toyotomi. It would also require new arrangements for military spending, shipping and overseas defence. The decision rests with [ROOT.GetCountry.GetRuler.GetFullName].

Japan asks to retain its unified government. [SCOPE.sCharacter('nesnd_japan_commander').GetFullName] has been charged with preparing the expedition. Former western officers will leave the mainland with their commander, supported by the fleet, treasury and allied Japanese lords. Victory would provide territories for the Emperor and Tokugawa. The court must now decide whether to pursue the terms by force.

The settlement in Japan is in force. The Toyotomi retain Chugoku and the remainder of Kansai; the Tokugawa take Edo and the northern domains. Kyoto and Osaka recognize the Emperor, with a regent conducting Wa’s government. Wu administers Kyushu and Shikoku directly. The new governments take charge of local revenues and armies, dividing the resources once commanded by the Toyotomi.
The conflict has ended without implementation of the partition. Fleets and garrisons will redeploy under the existing borders and agreements.

Honshu now answers to one independent government. [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] is bringing the revenues and armies of the former domains under common authority. Merchants in the castle towns await a settlement of tolls and taxes as they prepare to trade beyond the old domain boundaries.
Keep the current borders and Japanese government; retain resources for the mainland and other overseas commitments.

#bold Territorial settlement#!\nJapanese Kyushu and Shikoku pass to Wu. Tokugawa Fu receives Kanto and existing northern Japanese holdings; Imperial Wa receives Kyoto and Osaka. Toyotomi retains the rest of Kansai, Chugoku and Korean holdings. New states become Wu protectorates. An independent Toyotomi state also becomes a protectorate; an existing subject relationship is retained. #v Foreign territory is not transferred.#!
Be independent and fully own Honshu’s seven regions: Kanto, Kyoto, Kansai, Chugoku, Tokai, Tohoku and Hokushinetsu.

Alliances across the strait once helped the Toyotomi conquer their rivals and allowed the mainland court to intervene in Japan’s successions, domains and wars. Taxes, armies and commerce now follow competing authorities. [ROOT.GetCountry.GetName] must reunite Honshu and secure the freedom to govern its own affairs.
Unite Honshu under an independent government.
Divide authority among the Emperor, Toyotomi and Tokugawa.

Nonnegative income and bureaucracy; legitimacy at least 50; army and naval projection at least Japan's; a nonzero fleet with at least 90% maintenance fulfillment. Neither country may be at war or committed to a diplomatic play, nor have a mutual truce. Japan must fully own Kanto, Kyoto, Kansai and Chugoku. Japan must retain a Toyotomi monarchy, with Fu and Wa not yet existing.

If Japan is a Wu subject, it will become independent as the [concept_diplomatic_play] begins. Wu demands the reorganization of Japan; Japan demands Wu’s humiliation. #v The territorial settlement takes effect only if Wu’s war goal is enforced.#!
Withdraw the current programme and end the government’s reform campaign. Reform progress is lost, and reforms cannot be proposed again for #v 24#! months. Existing laws and buildings remain.
Fund the advocates of reform so that their proposals can more quickly become law.

Arsenals and shipyards bring military spending into the towns. Contractors want dependable orders; officers resent having to bargain over the price of their equipment. As the workshops grow, these negotiations are becoming part of the business of government.

The ports bring the prices of distant markets into the countryside. Cotton, silk and tea have found new buyers, and both landowners and merchants want a larger share of the proceeds. The work of rural households is increasingly governed by decisions made far from their villages.

The dynasty can bring loyal retainers and reformers together. Preserve the crown, appoint capable officials, and give representative deliberation and enterprise a place in the state.\n\nThe policy cannot be changed for #v 12#! months. Changing policy resets reform progress.

The army needs a common command, and the state needs orders that can be carried through. Back the officers in reorganizing recruitment and supply, drawing provincial manpower and revenues into a common defence.\n\nThe policy cannot be changed for #v 12#! months. Changing policy resets reform progress.

Public trust in the government is faltering, and local divisions are deepening.

The domains of the shogunate, rural clans and merchants of the castle towns once upheld their own local orders. Schools and public administration connect distant communities, while flourishing commerce ties more livelihoods together. Security at home and the country’s fortunes in war shape confidence in a shared future.

Food, furniture and household goods are finding customers beyond the wealthiest homes. Their manufacturers have acquired a reason to care about ordinary incomes. Families struggling to feed themselves have little to spend on other goods, limiting sales and putting pressure on prices and profits.
Constitutional reform proceeds under the crown.

The old retainers want reform carried out in the monarch’s name. Merchants and officials trained in the new schools seek legal protection from arbitrary levies and local power. The crown can bring them together, but their respective rights remain to be settled.
We shall decide our own affairs.

Foreign envoys now deal directly with our government. Defence and overseas affairs, once conducted through an overlord, rest on institutions of our own.\n\nThe merchants and local leaders who supported independence have not retired from public life. They have brought new petitions, expecting the government to honour its promises.

New arrangements for appointing officials are in place, and the laws have changed how power is distributed. Families accustomed to holding local office by birth must now contend with positions and powers defined by the state. Officials, soldiers and merchants who took part in reform are finding their places within these arrangements, which now guide the conduct of public affairs.

The court has settled new arrangements for representation and public office. The monarch still has the company of old retainers, but provincial administration is admitting officials with a different education.\n\nReformers loyal to the crown believe these concessions will preserve the monarchy. Whether those who have gained a voice will be satisfied remains an open question.

The officers have secured the centralized government they sought. Recruitment, training and supplies come under common direction, and local officials must carry out the government’s orders. Arsenals and tool workshops equip the expanded army, giving the military administration the means to enforce its policy in the provinces.

Those entitled to vote now choose their representatives, and newspapers can debate the conduct of government. Officials face new rules of appointment, while political argument has spread beyond the old ruling families.\n\nSchools are bringing more people into this world. How the next generation will use these rights is theirs to decide.
Our envoy is awaiting a reply.

Edo now governs extensive northern territories. Garrisons can hold the roads, but they cannot conduct every part of provincial administration. The government needs officials to organise its revenue and spending, while the castle towns must accommodate merchants, craftsmen and people seeking work away from home. A country capable of sustaining ordinary government will be better placed to seek greater powers.

The courtiers of Kyoto and the merchants of Osaka have different connections and interests. Courtly rank does not pay soldiers, and private wealth does not become public revenue of its own accord. Officials must organise taxation and administration in the territories they govern so that the towns can sustain the new government.

Partition has deprived the Toyotomi retainers of their former authority over Japan, but the troops and households remaining in the west still need support. Old prestige cannot settle who collects the revenue or conducts local government. A dependable administration must be established in the surviving territories, with castle towns serving as centres of government, taxation and employment.
The country has established a functioning provincial administration.

The grain trade brings customers, and craftsmen and apprentices settle near them. New neighbourhoods need schools; offices and booksellers need paper. Town institutions are taking on duties once left to village households and clans.

The towns need food that can be stored and carried over long distances. Grain and fish merchants want customers beyond the harvest season. Canning offers a way to combine purchasing, processing and transport in one business, while food factories could provide work after the harvest is over.

Harvests, fishing boats and grain merchants sustain life in the towns. When food prices rise, complaints from the markets soon reach the authorities. The government must keep food coming into the towns at prices their people can afford.

Aid from the mainland court helped the Toyotomi subdue Japan, binding tribute and maritime trade to the politics of the islands. Greater autonomy touches an overlord’s revenue, naval interests and influence in Japan. Those interests endure even when the old obligations are dissolved.

The Standing of an Independent State
The country may seek foreign assistance and union on its own behalf. Envoys may be sent once every #v 6#! months.

Honshu has been reunited, but the question of Kyushu and Shikoku remains unsettled. Their ports and sea routes matter to trade and defence in southern Japan. The government may seek the remaining territories or accept the existing borders and relinquish its claims.
Relinquish our territorial claims to Kyushu and Shikoku and accept the current borders.
Territorial questions in Korea remain open to negotiation.
Local councils take part in civil administration and education.
Governors direct taxation and civil administration in our Korean territories.

The mines and ports of southern Korea sustain trade across the strait. Local merchants depend on those routes, while provincial elites resist surrendering civil affairs to officials from across the sea. Arguments often come down to who will control the next levy.
The government has yet to settle how its Korean territories will be administered.
Bring local councils into civil administration and education, seeking local cooperation to ease resistance to our rule.\n\nKorean policy cannot be changed again for #v 24#! months.

Offer a settlement to Korea or its overlord. If accepted, our holdings in Busan and Yangho will pass to Korea, and we will relinquish our claims to both regions.\n\nEnvoys may be sent once every #v 6#! months.

Appoint governors to centralize taxation and civil administration in our Korean territories, giving the government closer control over local revenue and affairs.\n\nKorean policy cannot be changed again for #v 24#! months.

Families who have found work in the mills must still pay rent, buy food and find money for their children’s schooling. They have brought labour and tax revenue to the towns, and expect a share in their prosperity. The promise of a better life will be judged against these everyday expenses.

Replace seclusion with mercantilism and permit overseas commerce. The common market’s tariffs remain under the control of its leading country.

The castle town grew around the lord’s fortress and the homes of his retainers. Now workers, apprentices and shopkeepers are settling in new streets, with children who need schooling. A town built to serve its lord is becoming a society with demands of its own.
Centralize authority and reorganize the army and its supplies.

The officers regard the army as the country’s most dependable institution. They seek common control over recruitment, training and supplies, bringing provincial forces under national direction. Arsenals and tool workshops would equip this army, while a concentrated government could carry the officers’ programme into the provinces.

Collecting taxes and raising soldiers were once the duties of the warrior class. Mining and manufacturing require merchants as well. The mineral wealth of the north gives Edo new revenues, but also new partners: men without swords who are growing wealthy and expect the government to protect their businesses.

The country governs its own domestic and foreign affairs.

The promises made in pursuit of independence now confront the government. Who will pay for defence, who will set the tariffs, and how much authority will remain in local hands? Those who contributed money and those who served expect a place in the new state.
The country is a subject again, with foreign affairs constrained by its overlord.

Hereditary warriors and local loyalties sustained the old armies, with recruitment and training varying between domains. The country needs organized manpower, trained officers and forces that answer to a common command. Whether defence rests on a standing army or a national militia, military service must support the affairs of the nation.

Tributary ties and maritime restrictions once placed diplomacy and trade within an overlord’s arrangements. We need to open our ports, send out merchant ships and negotiate with other countries in our own name. Lasting sovereignty will give these exchanges a government they can rely upon.

Japan’s overseas trade has long been confined to a few designated ports by strict prohibitions. Merchants seek distant raw materials and wider markets for their produce. The government must arrange the opening of the ports and confront those whose influence rests on the old restrictions.

After the Toyotomi unified Japan, the authority of the court, the armies of the domains and the commerce of Osaka sustained the shogunate. New wealth and learning are changing these relationships. Merchants, officers and scholars seek a greater say in government, challenging the old arrangements for appointing officials, commanding troops and making laws.
Open the sea routes to obtain the materials our factories need, while using tariffs to support domestic producers in the wider market.
Adopt protectionist trade laws and open our ports. The common market’s tariffs remain under the control of its leading country.
